claims.text: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 can contain ordered B2 and disordered FCC phases.
The initial AlCoCrFeNi2.1 microstructure is nanolamellar.
The as-cast or solution-treated alloy has high initial ductility.
Classical grain-boundary embrittlement is absent during aging at 400–700 °C.
Aging at 400–700 °C is sufficient to evolve local chemical order in the B2 phase.
The 400–700 °C aging range is below the decomposition temperature of a single-phase FCC alloy.
The B2 structure remains ordered while local chemical orders evolve during intermediate aging.
Local chemical order within B2 increases lattice resistance and Peierls stress for dislocation glide.
LCO evolution creates strong, coherent phase boundaries that impede dislocation motion.
Intermediate-aging LCO development raises the critical resolved shear stress for slip.
Dislocations become unable to cross phase boundaries or ordered domains at intermediate aging conditions.
Blocked dislocation transmission causes the transient loss of ductility.
At higher aging temperatures, LCOs dissolve or coarsen, or phase boundaries become more compliant through disordering.
The high-temperature changes permit dislocation bypass and restore ductility.
Ductility should vary non-monotonically with aging temperature and exhibit a sharp intermediate-temperature minimum.
The ductility minimum coincides with peak LCO strengthening and the strongest phase-boundary barrier effect.
The as-cast or solution-treated baseline is ductile because strong LCOs are absent and dislocations can glide through FCC and weakly ordered B2.
The embrittlement regime is bounded approximately by 400–700 °C, where LCOs are stable and strong but have not dissolved or coarsened significantly.
Observation of the ductile-brittle-ductile transition without corresponding LCO or phase-boundary evolution would falsify the hypothesis.
A correlation of embrittlement with grain coarsening or impurity segregation rather than LCO evolution would falsify the proposed mechanism.
